reasoning: Age 3 years with fever (38.5°C) since last night and ear pulling is classic for acute otitis media; however, cannot exclude serious bacterial infection (SBI) in a febrile young child without definitive exam and labs.
Vital signs are age-appropriate tachycardia (HR 128) and tachypnea (RR 26) for a 3-year-old with fever; SpO2 98% is reassuring. Temperature of 38.5°C is moderate fever.
Responsiveness is alert; no signs of altered mental status, no reported rash, no stated difficulty breathing. Pain score 4/10 is moderate.

Critical ESI decision point: This is a febrile young child WITHOUT prior medical record (immunization status unknown, no baseline data). ESI Handbook p.29 emphasizes that incomplete immunization status in a febrile child warrants consideration of high-risk categorization and possible isolation.

Although the presentation is consistent with simple otitis media (localized ear finding), the combination of (a) young age, (b) fever, (c) no prior records to establish immunization or medical history, and (d) inability to completely exclude SBI (occult UTI, bacteremia, meningitis) clinically at triage mandates high-risk assignment.
At least two resources will be needed: urinalysis/urine culture, blood work/culture, likely imaging or specialist exam. Meets ESI-3 resource threshold, but high-risk presentation elevates to ESI-2.
ESI-2 is appropriate: high-risk condition (febrile child with unknown baseline and immunization status) who should not wait, even though currently stable-appearing.
red_flags: Age 3 years + fever + unknown immunization status
No prior medical record on file—cannot rule out occult serious bacterial infection
Tachycardia and tachypnea age-appropriate but consistent with systemic infection
Irritability in young child with fever can indicate meningitis or other invasive disease
Ear findings alone do not exclude concurrent UTI, bacteremia, or CNS infection in this age group
